channel.title: The Librarian's Regimen
channel.description: Notes on health, nutrition and medicine, worked through one question at a time from the primary literature: what the studies actually found, how sure anyone can honestly be, and what that leaves a reasonable person to do. Written by a reader, not a clinician — nothing here is medical advice.

item.title: Why Are Tattoos Permanent, and Where Does the Ink Actually Go?
item.description: A tattoo needle deposits ink once, in seconds, and the picture stays for decades. The obvious explanation — the ink just sits inertly in your skin cells — is wrong. What actually holds it there is your immune system, running a relay that never stops, and part of the ink doesn't stay in the skin at all.

item.title: Do Calcium and Vitamin D Supplements Actually Prevent Fractures and Falls?
item.description: A BMJ systematic review of 69 randomised trials and 153,902 adults found calcium alone, vitamin D alone, and the two combined all produced little to no meaningful reduction in fractures or falls. One combination did clear statistical significance — but missed the review's own bar for a clinically meaningful benefit, and the signal traces largely to a single 1992 French nursing-home trial. Here is what the numbers say, outcome by outcome, and why "statistically significant" and "worth taking" turned out to be two different questions.

item.title: Folate vs. Folic Acid: What's the Difference, and What Does the Evidence Say About Autism?
item.description: "Folate" and "folic acid" get used as if they're the same word, and they aren't quite the same molecule. Here's the actual biochemical difference, why folic acid ended up in bread in the first place, and what a genuinely active — and fast-moving — body of research says about folate and autism, including a striking but very small 2026 pilot trial.

item.title: The First Blood Test for Fifty Cancers Reached the FDA Today. It Still Misses Most Early Ones
item.description: A tweet promoting a podcast with oncologist Azra Raza asks whether medicine should chase cancer's first cell instead of its last. The technology closest to doing that, GRAIL's Galleri blood test, had its first-ever FDA advisory panel hearing today. What it actually finds, what a 142,942-person trial found it missing, and how far Dr. Raza's own, more radical idea still has to go.

item.title: Why Do IBD Patients Relapse Even in Remission?
item.description: A WEHI-led study of roughly 900 gut biopsies from 80 people, published in Science, finds that intestinal cells in inflammatory bowel disease patients can stay primed for an inflammatory kind of cell death even during symptom-free remission — and the stronger that signal, the higher the relapse risk over the following two years. Ordinary gut lining renews itself through cell death constantly; here's what's actually different about this one, and what the study can and can't say about a healthy gut.

item.title: A Drug for Hair Loss That Clears Aging Cells Instead of Blocking a Hormone
item.description: A biotech company is about to put the first GPX4-modulating "senolytic" into a human trial for male pattern hair loss, after ex vivo human follicle data that matched or beat finasteride. It's a genuinely new mechanism after nearly thirty years of the same two drugs — but the data so far is six days old, from follicles in a dish, not scalps.

item.title: Does Light at Night Hurt Your Heart?
item.description: A UK Biobank study of 11,071 adults found that people with bedroom light above roughly 3 lux at night — dimmer than almost any lamp, but bright enough for closed eyes to register — developed a thicker, stiffer-pumping heart and higher rates of heart failure, stroke and atrial fibrillation years later than people who slept in real darkness. Led by Tulane's Lu Qi, published September 9, 2026 in the European Heart Journal. Here's what "3 lux" actually looks like, and what the study can and can't say about a nightstand lamp.

item.title: Does Red Light Therapy Work, and Why Does the Price Range From $60 to $1,200?
item.description: Red light therapy panels run from about $50 for a handheld unit to well over $1,200 for a full-body array, all promising some version of the same benefits. The clinical evidence is genuinely strong for exactly one use case that has nothing to do with a home panel, real but modest for a couple of things people actually buy these for, and weak or backwards for most of what gets marketed. And independent measurement has found $1,200 panels overstating their light output by roughly the same margin as $60 ones.

item.title: Does Stopping a GLP-1 Drug Raise Your Heart Risk?
item.description: A Veterans Affairs study of 333,687 people with type 2 diabetes found that the longer someone went off a GLP-1 drug like semaglutide, the higher their risk of stroke, heart attack or death climbed — 4% higher at six months off, 14% at a year, 22% at two years — compared with staying on it, and restarting the drug only partly closed the gap. Here's what the study actually measured, and the one comparison group that changes how the headline number should be read.

item.title: Alexander Disease, and the First Drug Approved to Treat It
item.description: What is Alexander disease, and what did the FDA actually approve for it? AxD is an ultra-rare, usually fatal genetic disorder of the brain's astrocytes, caused by mutations in the GFAP gene. On September 3, 2026, the FDA approved Zanvastro (zilganersen), an RNA-targeted drug given by quarterly spinal injection, as the first treatment aimed at the disease itself rather than its symptoms. The trial behind it enrolled 49 randomized patients.

item.title: Do Common Food Preservatives Raise Blood Pressure and Heart Risk?
item.description: A French cohort of 112,395 adults, followed a median of 7.9 years, found that the heaviest consumers of preservative food additives developed hypertension and cardiovascular disease at higher rates than the lightest. Eight individual preservatives were each tied to high blood pressure, including sodium nitrite, potassium sorbate, citric acid and — oddly — ascorbic acid, plain vitamin C. This is a cohort study, so it shows association, not proof of cause. Here is what the numbers actually say, and how the eight show up on an American ingredient panel.

item.title: The First Approved Treatment for Ataxia in Ataxia-Telangiectasia
item.description: What is ataxia-telangiectasia, and does the drug the FDA just approved for it actually work? A-T is a rare, inherited disorder in a DNA-repair gene that causes progressive loss of coordination starting in early childhood. On September 18, 2026, the FDA approved levacetylleucine (Aqneursa) as the first treatment for the ataxia itself, based on a 73-patient trial showing a real, statistically significant improvement on the standard ataxia rating scale.

item.title: Pancreatic Cancer Has a Drug That Works. Now the FDA Wants It Tried First
item.description: Three weeks after approving daraxonrasib for pancreatic cancer that has already been treated — the first drug to roughly double survival in that disease — the FDA gave it Breakthrough Therapy status for newly diagnosed patients, on top of chemotherapy. What the drug does, what the trials actually showed, what "breakthrough" legally means, and the $39,800-a-month company behind it.

item.title: What Radioligand Therapy Is, and Why a Second Lutathera Matters
item.description: On September 14 the FDA approved Bexlutry, Curium's copy of Novartis's Lutathera — the first "radioligand equivalent" ever cleared. The question underneath the headline: what is a radioligand therapy, what does the evidence say it does for neuroendocrine tumours, and why did it take a Delaware courtroom to get a second one to market? With numbers, and the companies.

item.title: What a Kidney Stone Actually Is, and Why It Forms
item.description: About one adult in ten will make a kidney stone. Before the questions about water, calcium and what to eat, the first one: what a stone actually is, what it is made of, and why it forms in some kidneys and not others — read from the studies. With a postscript on hard water, distillers, and calcium pills.
